mechanisms.definition: Missingness depends systematically on other observed variables in the dataset, but not on the missing value itself.
mechanisms.taxi_context: Illustrative: Missing congestion surcharge fields in trips originating outside Manhattan congestion zones.

mechanisms.definition: Missingness depends directly on the unobserved missing value itself or unmeasured factors.
mechanisms.taxi_context: Illustrative: Unreported cash tips where passengers pay cash directly to the driver without recording.

standard_scaler.description: Transforms features to have zero mean (μ=0) and unit standard deviation (σ=1).
standard_scaler.outlier_sensitivity: High — Outliers skew the mean and expand standard deviation, compressing non-outliers into a narrow band.

minmax_scaler.description: Compresses features strictly into the bounded range [0, 1].
minmax_scaler.outlier_sensitivity: Very High — Extreme outliers set x_max or x_min, squashing the vast majority of regular data into a minuscule sub-interval.

robust_scaler.description: Centers data around the median (median=0) and divides by IQR (IQR=1). Does not cap bounds.
robust_scaler.outlier_sensitivity: Low / Robust — Outliers do not distort the median or the middle 50% spread, preserving distribution shape without collapsing typical records.

leakage_demonstration.verdict: Fitting the scaler on the entire dataset incorporates test-set distribution parameters (μ, σ) into training preprocessing. In production or cross-validation, this produces overly optimistic validation performance and causes pipeline drift on genuine unseen data.

comparison_matrix.outlier_impact: High. Outliers distort mean & variance, compressing non-outlier cluster.
comparison_matrix.recommended_use: Features following roughly Gaussian distributions; Gradient Descent algorithms; Ridge/Lasso regularization; PCA; Logistic Regression.

comparison_matrix.outlier_impact: Severe. Extreme outliers push x_max far out, squeezing valid data into a narrow sliver.
comparison_matrix.recommended_use: Algorithms requiring strictly bounded inputs (Image pixel values, Neural Networks with Sigmoid activations, KNN distance where bounded range is required and outliers are absent).

comparison_matrix.outlier_impact: Low / Robust. Uses 50th percentile and middle 50% range; extreme values cannot skew center or spread.
comparison_matrix.recommended_use: Heavy-tailed, skewed datasets with persistent genuine outliers (e.g., NYC Taxi trip distances, airport fares, surge rates) where removing outliers is undesirable.

models_needing_scaling.why_needed: Compute Euclidean or Manhattan distances between vectors. A feature with larger magnitude (e.g. Total Fare in $ vs Passenger Count in units) completely dominates the distance metric, rendering smaller-scale features negligible.

models_needing_scaling.examples: Simple & Multiple Linear Regression (GD), Logistic Regression, Neural Networks
models_needing_scaling.why_needed: Unscaled features create elongated, elliptical cost surface contours. Gradient descent oscillates wildly and requires an excessively small learning rate to converge. Scaling produces circular loss contours, accelerating convergence.
Regularization penalizes weight magnitudes (λ ∑ w_i²). If features have unequal scales, the penalty disproportionately punishes coefficients of smaller-scale features, biasing feature selection.

models_needing_scaling.examples: SVM (Support Vector Machines), PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
models_needing_scaling.why_needed: SVM maximizes the margin in feature space; unscaled attributes distort the margin boundary. PCA identifies axes of maximum variance; unscaled high-variance features falsely capture all principal components.

models_not_needing_scaling.why_not_needed: Tree algorithms split nodes feature-by-feature based on threshold inequalities (x_i <= threshold) evaluated via Gini Impurity, Entropy, or MSE reduction. Monotonic transformations do not change the ranking or split points of single features.

Like Random Forests, boosting algorithms construct ensembles of decision tree stumps/leaves. Split searching operates independently along each 1D coordinate, making them completely invariant to monotonic feature scaling.
Count-based frequency probability distributions evaluate class likelihoods independently for categorical inputs.

treatment_comparison.description: Drop records sharing identical [tpep_pickup_datetime, tpep_dropoff_datetime, PULocationID, ...].
treatment_comparison.risk_assessment: High Risk. NYC TLC data intentionally excludes Medallion/Hack License IDs for privacy. Two cabs leaving JFK at the same minute to Midtown are legitimate independent trips. Deleting them creates artificial revenue undercounting.

risks.explanation: Official NYC TLC public parquet files intentionally anonymize or omit taxi medallion numbers and hack license IDs to protect driver privacy. Consequently, two distinct taxis operated by different drivers that pick up passengers at the exact same location and time cannot be distinguished by timestamps alone.

Major transit hubs (JFK Terminal 4, LaGuardia Terminal B, Penn Station, Grand Central, Yankee Stadium) experience dozens of taxi departures per minute. Two cabs departing simultaneously toward the Financial District with 1 passenger each represent legitimate independent commercial rides.

Taximeter clocks in disparate vehicles may round pickup times to the nearest minute or second. Trips initiated within seconds of each other in the same zone often appear to have identical pickup times.
Dropping subset duplicates artificially depresses total fare volume, passenger counts, and congestion metrics, distorting public transit planning and revenue forecasts.

duplicates.verdict: Exact row duplicates are 0 (0.00%) in the cleaned dataset. Subset duplicates (2 records, 0.00007%) share timestamps and zones but represent legitimate distinct rides. Main cleaned dataset is retained intact at 2,816,149 records.

educational_theory.why_regularization_helps: In high-dimensional or collinear feature spaces, Ordinary Least Squares minimizes in-sample training error without regard to parameter magnitude. This leads to large, oscillating weights that fit statistical noise rather than the true underlying data-generating distribution. Regularization introduces a penalty on parameter complexity into the loss function: Loss = Empirical Error + Complexity Penalty. This shrinks coefficients, stabilizes variance, and prevents catastrophic overfitting on unseen test records.
educational_theory.alpha_parameter_intuition: The regularization strength α (alpha) governs the Bias-Variance tradeoff: When α = 0, the penalty is disabled, yielding standard unconstrained OLS (high variance, low bias). As α increases, the penalty forces coefficients toward zero, reducing model complexity and variance at the expense of adding bias. If α is excessively large, coefficients are shrunk near zero, leading to severe underfitting.
educational_theory.l1_vs_l2_geometry: L1 (Lasso) vs L2 (Ridge) Geometric Duality: Ridge's L2 constraint region is a smooth hypersphere (∑ wⱼ² ≤ C). The elliptical contours of the MSE loss typically intersect the sphere along curved boundaries, shrinking all weights proportionally without setting them strictly to zero. Lasso's L1 constraint region is a sharp diamond / cross-polytope (∑ |wⱼ| ≤ C) with vertices located directly on the coordinate axes. The loss contours frequently intersect at these sharp corners, forcing coefficients to exactly zero and performing automatic feature selection.
educational_theory.polynomial_overfitting_risks: Why Polynomial Regression Can Overfit: Polynomial regression projects features into higher-order powers [x, x², x³, ..., xᵈ]. While degree 2 models natural tapering of fare rates over longer hauls, degrees ≥ 3 introduce Runge's phenomenon: extreme oscillations near the edges of the feature support. The model twists to pass through outlier data points in the training set, causing MSE on unseen test data to explode.
